raw_response:
I am 45 and have worked these 9 mu since I was 15. My family has seven mouths to feed, so I cannot gamble everything on cash crops. I know this soil. I will put 7 mu into my wheat-maize double crop because that gives me grain for the table and steady income. The remaining 2 mu goes to cotton for cash, but no more—cotton needs too much picking labor, and my parents are old.

My wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. I use improved seeds from the county supply store—they are not the most expensive, but they survive the winter here and I know them. I will top-dress nitrogen twice this spring, about 18 kg per mu in total, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate three times from my well: at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. Water costs electricity, so I do not waste it, but wheat needs water at these stages. Two sprays will handle the aphids and rust that always come.

After wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately rotary till and plant hybrid maize seed. Timing is everything—you lose yield for every day you delay. Maize gets about 16 kg nitrogen per mu, and less phosphorus and potassium than wheat. I will irrigate twice if the summer turns dry, and spray for weeds and corn borers.

For the 2 mu of cotton, I will plough deep because cotton roots need loose soil. I plant hybrid Bt cotton to save on pesticide for bollworms, but I still need three sprays for mites and aphids. Cotton needs more potassium, so I apply 8 kg per mu. Three irrigations during flowering and boll formation will do it.

I expect wheat to yield around 450 kg per mu, maize about 520 kg per mu, and seed cotton about 260 kg per mu. These are honest numbers—not my best years, not my worst.
